observation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems can handle simple dialogue tasks, but complex tasks remain difficult because naively chaining LLMs induces cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies. Real-world LLM agent frameworks tend to oversimplify the complexities of collaborative problem solving and often rely on unstructured natural-language dialogue, which loses information across rounds and produces unproductive chatter. Existing code-generation methods also lack self-correction mechanisms that verify runtime executability, leaving complex software engineering tasks unmet.

claims: LLM-based multi-agent applications are frequently built as systems of conversational agents that exchange natural-language messages; AutoGen is a canonical framework for such conversations, and ChatDev instantiates the idea for collaborative software development.

In these conversation-centric designs, the agentic state is carried by the message history rather than by a structured external artifact, so false or off-topic content from an early turn can be propagated to all later agents.

works.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development

claims: Several frameworks address the weaknesses of fully open-ended dialogue by imposing process structure: ChatDev organizes role-played chat along a software-waterfall lifecycle, and MetaGPT uses standardized operating procedures that assign concrete intermediate deliverables to roles.

MetaGPT explicitly motivates this structured decomposition as a way to reduce the cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies that arise when LLM-based agents are simply chained through unstructured dialogue.

works.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework

claims: A complementary body of work tries to improve the reliability of individual LLM outputs through multi-agent debate or self-refinement: independent LLM agents that read and critique each other's answers improve factuality and reasoning, and prompting for divergent multi-agent debate yields similar gains.

Self-refinement methods allow a model to revise its own generations from feedback, and Reflexion extends self-improvement by maintaining verbal self-reflections over episodes; these protocols nonetheless reason over unconstrained natural-language hypotheses rather than executable or formally checkable artifacts.

works.title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate
Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

claims: In code generation, execution has become an important feedback signal: CodeT samples candidate programs and generated tests and selects the candidates that pass those tests, while Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug shows that a model can repair code after reading compiler errors and unit-test failures.

These execution-guided methods are defined for a single code generator operating on self-contained programming problems, and they do not provide a runtime-verification protocol for multi-agent teams producing repository-scale code.

works.title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug

claims: Benchmarks that approximate real, long-horizon agent use confirm the remaining gap: AgentBench evaluates LLM agents across diverse interactive environments and shows that even the best models underperform substantially on tasks that require many steps and tool interactions.

At the repository level, SWE-bench measures models on real GitHub issues and reports very low patch-success rates; SWE-agent adds an agent-computer interface for browsing, editing, and running tests, which improves performance considerably but still leaves most repository-level software-engineering tasks unresolved.

works.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering

solution.idea:
The prior work collectively supports a diagnosis. AutoGen and ChatDev exemplify conversation-centric multi-agent systems in which agentic state is carried by message history; an early hallucination or off-topic statement can therefore become a hidden premise for every subsequent agent. MetaGPT introduces standardized operating procedures and concrete intermediate deliverables, but those deliverables are still mostly documentation, so they do not give the runtime an executable oracle with which to reject a bad deliverable before it propagates. Multi-agent debate, Self-Refine, and Reflexion strengthen individual-agent reasoning and self-correction, yet they reason over unconstrained natural-language hypotheses rather than artifacts whose correctness can be checked by a compiler, test runner, or integration suite. CodeT and Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug demonstrate the power of execution as feedback, but they cover a single code generator on self-contained programming problems and do not define a verification protocol for a multi-agent team operating on repository-scale code. AgentBench, SWE-bench, and SWE-agent confirm that long-horizon and repository-level tasks need tool use, executable feedback, and an agent-computer interface rather than simply more agents or more conversational rounds.

The proposed direction is a structured multi-agent protocol that makes executable runtime verification the gate between all stages. The design combines the strongest ideas from the related work: a ChatDev/MetaGPT-style lifecycle and role decomposition, CodeT-style candidate selection with generated tests, Teaching-LLMs-to-Self-Debug-style repair from compiler and test feedback, and a SWE-agent-style workspace for browsing, editing, and running code. The decisive change is that shared state is not conversation history; it is a versioned artifact repository containing requirements, interface specifications, code patches, tests, and execution reports. Every time an LLM-based role produces a contribution, the contribution is submitted as a patch to a specific artifact, and a deterministic coordinator applies the patch in a clean repository and runs the relevant executable checks. Only a contribution that passes the gate is marked verified and may be consumed by a later role. This blocks cascading hallucinations at their source: false, off-topic, or logically inconsistent content stays attached to the artifact that failed its runtime gate and is never propagated through a downstream prompt that reads a long dialogue transcript.

The core insight is to use two heterogeneous control mechanisms together: process structure governs who does what, while executability governs whether that work is correct. The natural-language debate and self-reflection methods can still be used inside an individual agent's reasoning or in a separate root-cause discussion, but their output is not trusted until encoded as a patch that passes tests. Alternatives were considered but rejected: a pure conversational framework may be simpler but has exactly the propagation failure identified in the observation; adding more self-refinement without an external runtime yields more fluent but still ungrounded hypotheses; and a monolithic top-down planner that writes the whole repository in one patch is too coarse because a complex failure cannot be attributed to a single role and a repair loop cannot isolate the offending module. The key trade-off of the chosen design is that it is more process-heavy than free-form agent chat: each deliverable must be transcribed into an artifact, and each handoff must survive a verification gate. The benefit is that repository-scale tasks are decomposed into units whose correctness can be attributed and whose failure can be repaired locally.
solution.implementation:
The implementation is an artifact-centric, runtime-verified SOP engine with the following components.

1. Artifact repository model. All persistent state lives in a versioned Git repository rather than in agent dialogue. Artifact types include: (a) `requirements/*.req` files, which encode user stories and acceptance criteria in a machine-readable key-value schema; (b) `interfaces/*.api` files, which contain compilable stub definitions, type signatures, and data schemas for each module boundary; (c) `issues/*.iss` records, each representing one decomposed work item with fields `id`, `module`, `owner_role`, `depends_on`, `acceptance_test`, and `state`; (d) `src/**` and `tests/**` for actual code and test executables; (e) `reports/*.rep` execution reports produced by the coordinator; and (f) a `manifest.lock` describing which versions of which artifacts are currently verified. Each generated file is versioned and immutable after commit; any change is a new revision with a parent pointer. A prompt given to any agent points only to relevant artifact revisions and to the latest runtime report on those revisions.

2. Role decomposition and coordination protocol. The coordinator is a deterministic process, not an LLM. It follows a fixed state machine that mirrors the life-cycle insight of ChatDev and MetaGPT while replacing conversational peer messages with scoped work orders. The phases are: requirements analysis, architecture and interface specification, unit implementation, unit verification, repository integration, and final acceptance. Role agents include a requirement analyst, an architect, implementers, a test engineer, an integration engineer, and an escalation architect. The coordinator uses the artifact dependency graph to decide which work item is ready. A work item is ready when all artifacts it depends on are already `verified`. For each ready item the coordinator spawns exactly the role that owns that item, with a bounded context consisting of: its issue record, the current verified interface specification, the acceptance test that defines success, and the most recent execution report from prior attempts of that issue. It deliberately does not include earlier conversation turns or unverified natural-language notes from other roles.

3. Agent workspace and message semantics. Each role agent runs in a sandboxed repository clone and interacts through an agent-computer interface modeled on SWE-agent. The allowed commands are `read_file`, `grep`, `edit_file`, `create_file`, `run_command`, and `submit`. All edited content must be expressed as a unified diff against a designated artifact path. There is no unstructured free-text channel between peers; what would be called a message in AutoGen is represented as a structured `issue_update` that changes an issue's state or appends a machine-readable note such as `request_interface_change_to=module B`. If a human-readable explanation is necessary, it is stored in an `explanation` field of the issue; downstream agents may read it for context, but downstream correctness gates never treat it as evidence of correctness.

4. Verification gate. The coordinator defines one central operation, `verify(patch, test_scope)`. It performs the following steps in a clean checkout: apply the patch; run syntax/import and static type checks; compile stub interface modules; execute the relevant unit tests generated for that work item; and, at integration phases, run the full repository test suite. The output is a structured execution report containing exit code, assertion messages, stack traces, names of failing tests, files and line numbers implicated, and which test scope was run. A patch is marked `verified` only if all applicable checks in its scope pass. If the gate fails, the patch is left unverified, the issue returns to a `repair` state, and the report is attached to the issue. Because the gate is deterministic and the patch is applied to a clean repository, a downstream agent never sees a contribution that has not actually executed successfully.

5. Unit-implementation and repair protocol. For each unit, the test engineer first creates and verifies an executable acceptance test derived from the requirement and interface schema. The implementation loop then proceeds in stages. In the candidate-generation stage, the implementer is asked to produce up to K candidate patches for the unit. The coordinator executes `verify` on each candidate independently in a fresh checkout. This extends CodeT's candidate-selection idea to a repository context: a candidate is acceptable only if it passes the frozen acceptance test and interface conformance checks. If multiple candidates pass, the tie is broken by smallest diff size, with the runtime test suite as the sole arbiter; no debate vote is used. If no candidate passes, the protocol enters the self-correction stage inspired by Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug: the implementer receives the structured report, is instructed to identify the root cause, and produces a new patch targeting only that error. This continues at most R rounds. If it still fails, the coordinator may launch a second independent repair agent with the same report to avoid fixation, and both repair candidates are again adjudicated by the runtime gate.

6. Escalation and interface repair. When a failing integration test points to an interface mismatch between two modules, the coordinator does not ask the agents to argue in natural language. It routes a structured `interface_bug` issue to the owner of the module whose API does not conform to the verified interface specification. The escalation architect may then edit the interface artifact, bump its version, mark all dependents unverified, and requeue the affected implementers with the new interface. The implementers receive the concrete diff of the changed interface and the failing runtime report. This ensures that architectural corrections are propagated as versioned, diff-able artifacts, not as conversational reinterpretations.

7. Repository integration and final gate. After all individual modules are marked verified, the integration engineer checks out the repository, applies the verified patches in topological dependency order, and runs an integration manifest containing cross-module tests and end-to-end smoke commands. If any integration test fails, the coordinator atomically bisects the failure by mapping stack frames and touched files to the responsible module, then creates a repair issue for that module. The final acceptance gate runs all unit and integration tests in a clean clone of the complete repository and requires that every issue used by the task is either `verified` or explicitly `blocked`, where `blocked` means that no downstream artifact depends on it and a report explains why it is out of scope. The final output is a single patch plus the verification report with the exact command invocations, test names, and pass/fail outcomes.

8. Key parameters. The protocol depends on configurable parameters rather than claims about tuned values: `K`, the number of independent candidate patches generated before selection; `R`, the maximum number of repair rounds for one implementer on one issue; `test_timeout`, the wall-clock limit for each runtime gate; `escalation_threshold`, the number of distinct repair hypotheses that must be tried before an interface-level escalation is permitted; and `stub_mode`, which determines whether unverified neighboring modules are represented by executable stubs during unit verification or are excluded until integration. These parameters control the trade-off between computational cost and isolation of failures; the coordinator uses no parameter derived from any experimental measurement, since none are yet available.

The whole design is closed-loop for code-carrying artifacts: every handoff is gated by execution, failures are converted into structured repair directives, and the repository, not the transcript, is the single source of truth. Unstructured natural-language debate and self-refinement can still occur, but only as internal reasoning or as explanatory notes attached to an issue; they never become the mechanism by which a module is accepted.
